questions.q: A before-update trigger fires in a synchronous transaction started by a user clicking Save. How many SOQL queries can the whole transaction issue before a LimitException?
questions.explain: Synchronous Apex allows 100 SOQL queries per transaction. The limit is shared by every trigger, flow-invoked Apex and class in that transaction.
wrong: 50 is the limit on future calls per transaction, not SOQL.
150 is the DML statement limit.
200 is the asynchronous SOQL limit.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A Batch Apex execute() method builds a large in-memory map and fails with a heap error. What is the heap limit the developer is working against?
options: 25 MB
10 MB
100 MB
60 MB
questions.explain: Batch Apex runs asynchronously, so each execute() transaction gets the asynchronous heap limit of 25 MB instead of the 10 MB synchronous limit. (Older study guides list 6 MB / 12 MB; the current Execution Governors and Limits page lists 10 MB / 25 MB.)
wrong: 10 MB is the synchronous heap limit.
100 MB is not an Apex heap limit.
60 is the async CPU limit in seconds, not heap in MB.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A shared utility method runs an optional enrichment query. It is called from triggers, batch jobs and LWC controllers. The developer wants it to skip the query when the transaction has no SOQL budget left. What should they do?
options: Wrap the query in try/catch and ignore System.LimitException.
Call OrgLimits.getMap() and skip the query when DailyApiRequests shows no remaining calls.
Hard-code a counter that stops after 100 queries.
Check Limits.getQueries() against Limits.getLimitQueries() first.
questions.explain: Limits.getQueries() returns queries used so far, and Limits.getLimitQueries() returns the cap for the current context (100 sync, 200 async), so the check works everywhere.
wrong: LimitException cannot be caught.
OrgLimits reports org-wide limits like API calls, not per-transaction SOQL.
A hard-coded 100 is wrong in async contexts (200) and ignores queries made by other code in the transaction.
questions.source: Apex Reference Guide: Limits Class

questions.q: A developer moves heavy logic from a trigger into a Queueable job. Which two limits are higher in the Queueable than in the synchronous trigger? Choose 2.
options: Total SOQL queries
Total DML statements
Maximum CPU time
Total rows retrieved by SOQL
Total callouts
questions.explain: Async Apex gets 200 SOQL queries (vs 100) and 60,000 ms CPU (vs 10,000 ms). Heap also rises (10 MB to 25 MB).
wrong: DML statements stay at 150 in both contexts.
Query rows stay at 50,000 in both contexts.
Callouts stay at 100 in both contexts.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A data load of 200 Contacts fails with "Too many SOQL queries: 101". What is the best fix?
options: Move the lookup into a @future method called once per Contact so each query runs in its own transaction.
Add LIMIT 1 to the query inside the loop.
Collect AccountIds in a Set, run one query into a Map<Id, Account>, then loop and read from the map.
Ask the admin to load Contacts in batches of 100.
questions.explain: Bulkified code queries once outside the loop and uses a Map for lookups, so it uses one SOQL query no matter how many records arrive.
wrong: 50 future calls max per transaction, and the description update in a before trigger would be lost.
LIMIT 1 still runs one query per record.
Smaller batches hide the bug instead of fixing it; API or UI paths can still send 200.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Bulk Apex Triggers

questions.q: A nightly process reads about 40,000 Case records and its heap usage is near the limit. What does switching to a SOQL for loop that iterates over List<Case> batches achieve?
options: It removes the 50,000 query row limit.
It runs the query asynchronously on another thread.
It lets the code run DML inside the loop on each chunk without counting against the 150-statement limit.
It retrieves records in chunks of 200, so the full result set is never held in heap at once.
questions.explain: SOQL for loops use efficient chunking (queryMore behind the scenes), so only a chunk of 200 records is in memory at a time, reducing heap usage.
wrong: Rows still count toward the 50,000 limit.
The loop runs synchronously in the same transaction.
DML inside the loop still counts toward 150 statements.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Working with Very Large SOQL Queries

questions.q: A developer needs fast lookups of Accounts by Id for records in Trigger.new. Which snippet is the most efficient?
options: Loop through a List<Account> each time a Contact needs its Account.
Map<Id, Account> m = new Map<Id, Account>([SELECT Id, Name FROM Account WHERE Id IN :ids]);
Query each Account inside the Contact loop with WHERE Id = :c.AccountId.
Use Database.query() with a string built inside the loop.
questions.explain: Passing a query result to the Map constructor builds an Id-keyed map in one query with O(1) lookups.
wrong: Nested list scans waste CPU time.
One query per record breaks the 100 SOQL limit.
Dynamic SOQL inside a loop still issues a query per iteration.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Maps of sObjects

questions.q: An after-insert trigger on Opportunity recalculates a Total_Won__c field on the parent Account. A 200-record load hits limits. Which two changes improve the code? Choose 2.
options: Call a @future method once per Opportunity so each Account update runs in its own transaction with fresh limits.
Replace the per-record query with one aggregate query: SUM(Amount) GROUP BY AccountId for all affected AccountIds.
Use Database.update(acc, false) instead of update.
Collect Account records in a Map<Id, Account> and issue a single update after the loop.
Add LIMIT 200 to the inner query.
questions.explain: One aggregate query replaces up to 200 queries and moves the summing to the database. Collecting Accounts in a map deduplicates them and allows one DML statement.
wrong: Up to 200 future calls exceeds the limit of 50 per transaction.
allOrNone=false changes error handling, not the number of DML statements.
LIMIT doesn't reduce the number of queries and could make totals wrong.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Bulk Apex Triggers; Aggregate Functions

questions.q: Which field on a custom object is indexed by default, with no help from Support?
options: A custom Text field
CreatedDate
A custom Picklist field
A Long Text Area field
questions.explain: CreatedDate is a standard indexed field, along with Id, Name, OwnerId, SystemModstamp, RecordTypeId and relationship fields.
wrong: Custom text fields are not indexed unless marked External ID/Unique or indexed by Support.
Picklists are not indexed by default.
Long Text Area fields cannot be indexed.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Working with Very Large SOQL Queries

questions.q: An object has 2,000,000 records. A query filters only on a custom field that has a custom index, and the filter matches 250,000 records. How will the optimizer most likely treat this filter?
options: Selective, because 250,000 is under the 333,333 cap.
Selective, because 250,000 is under 30% of 2,000,000.
Not selective, because the custom index threshold for 2M rows is 150,000 records.
Not selective, because custom indexes are never used on objects over 1M records.
questions.explain: Custom index threshold = 10% of the first 1M (100,000) + 5% of the next 1M (50,000) = 150,000. 250,000 exceeds it, so the index is skipped.
wrong: 333,333 is only the upper cap; the computed threshold here is lower.
30% applies to standard indexes, not custom ones.
Custom indexes are used on large objects when the filter is selective enough.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Working with Very Large SOQL Queries

questions.q: An object has 500,000 records. A report query filters on CreatedDate = LAST_N_DAYS:90, which matches 120,000 rows. Is the filter selective?
options: Yes. CreatedDate has a standard index, and 120,000 is under 30% of 500,000.
No. Date filters are never selective.
No. 120,000 is above 10% of 500,000 (50,000), the selectivity threshold for this filter.
Yes, but only if the query has an ORDER BY clause.
questions.explain: CreatedDate is a standard index. For a table under 1M rows, the standard threshold is 30%, which is 150,000 here.
wrong: Date fields with indexes can be selective.
10% is the custom index threshold; CreatedDate is a standard index.
ORDER BY does not decide selectivity.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Working with Very Large SOQL Queries

questions.q: A trigger queries Shipment__c (5 million rows) with WHERE Tracking_Code__c = :code. Tracking_Code__c is a plain, non-indexed Text field, and the trigger fails with a non-selective query error. Which two actions can fix it? Choose 2.
options: Add ORDER BY Tracking_Code__c to the query.
Mark Tracking_Code__c as an External ID so it is indexed.
Change the filter to LIKE '%' + code.
Add another selective, indexed filter such as a lookup Id or a narrow CreatedDate range that matches the business rule.
Rewrite the query as dynamic SOQL with Database.query() so the optimizer builds a fresh plan for each call.
questions.explain: An External ID field gets a custom index. Adding another selective indexed filter lets the optimizer use that index. Either can make the query selective.
wrong: Sorting does not make a filter selective.
A leading wildcard prevents index use.
Dynamic SOQL runs through the same optimizer.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Working with Very Large SOQL Queries

questions.q: In the Developer Console Query Plan tool, the best plan for a query shows a Cost of 2.4. What does this mean?
options: The query uses 2.4 seconds of CPU time.
The query is selective and will use an index.
The query will consume 2.4% of the SOQL row limit.
The query is not selective; the optimizer expects it to be slow.
questions.explain: A cost above 1 means the plan is not selective. Selective plans have a cost below 1.
wrong: Cost is a relative number, not seconds.
Selective plans have a cost under 1.
Cost is not tied to governor limits.
questions.source: Developer Console Query Plan Tool FAQ

questions.q: Name is indexed on Account. Which WHERE clause is least able to use that index?
options: Name = 'Acme Corp'
Name IN ('Acme', 'Globex')
Name LIKE '%corp'
Name LIKE 'Acme%'
questions.explain: A leading wildcard means the index can't be scanned by prefix, so the optimizer falls back to scanning. A trailing wildcard can still use the index.
wrong: Equality on an indexed field can use the index.
IN with a short list can use the index.
A trailing wildcard still allows index range scans.
questions.source: Query & Search Optimization Cheat Sheet

questions.q: A query on a 3M-row object filters WHERE Region__c = null. Region__c has a custom index, but the query is slow. What explains it and what helps?
options: Custom indexes exclude nulls by default. Ask Support for an index that includes nulls, or store a default value instead.
Null filters are always selective on custom-indexed fields, so the slowness must come from network latency or page rendering.
Region__c must be converted to a formula field to be indexed.
The index only works when the query uses SOSL.
questions.explain: By default custom indexes do not contain nulls, so "= null" can't use them. Support can build one that includes nulls, or a default value avoids nulls.
wrong: Null filters on custom-indexed fields are a common cause of table scans.
Formula fields are harder, not easier, to index (they must be deterministic).
SOSL uses the search index, not field indexes, and does not solve this.
questions.source: Best Practices for Deployments with Large Data Volumes

questions.q: Reports on a 20M-row custom object are slow because they always read the same 12 fields, and the object's standard and custom fields live in separate tables. A skinny table is proposed. Which statement is accurate?
options: A developer can create it in Setup and add parent Account fields to it.
Salesforce Support creates it, and the platform keeps it in sync with the source object.
It is copied to every sandbox type automatically on refresh.
It removes the need for selective filters, because every query against a skinny table is treated as indexed.
questions.explain: Skinny tables are enabled by Salesforce Support, hold fields from a single object to avoid joins, and are kept in sync automatically.
wrong: Developers can't create them, and they can't contain fields from other objects.
They copy automatically only to Full sandboxes.
Skinny tables reduce joins; selectivity still matters.
questions.source: Best Practices for Deployments with Large Data Volumes

questions.q: At roughly what point does Salesforce consider a single user to have ownership skew on an object?
options: More than 1,000 records
More than 2,000 records
More than 10,000 records
More than 1,000,000 records
questions.explain: Salesforce guidance flags ownership skew when one user owns more than about 10,000 records of an object.
wrong: Too low to cause skew problems.
2,000 is the SOSL row limit, not a skew threshold.
Problems appear well before 1M.
questions.source: Designing Record Access for Enterprise Scale

questions.q: An integration user owns 400,000 Account records. Each time the admin moves that user to a different role, sharing recalculation runs for hours. What should the architect recommend?
options: Give the integration user the System Administrator profile.
Split the Accounts into two record types.
Change the Account OWD to Public Read/Write and move the user into a mid-level role under the sales VP.
Assign the user no role, or an isolated role at the top of the hierarchy, and avoid changing it.
questions.explain: For unavoidable ownership skew, keeping the owner out of the hierarchy (or alone at the top) prevents expensive sharing recalculation when roles change.
wrong: Profile permissions don't affect sharing recalculation from role moves.
Record types don't affect ownership-based sharing.
Changing OWD is a big security change, and placing the user mid-hierarchy keeps the recalculation risk.
questions.source: Designing Record Access for Enterprise Scale

questions.q: A nightly Bulk API job loads 3 million Order__c records that look up to a small set of Account records. Many batches fail with UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW. Which two actions reduce the errors? Choose 2.
options: Increase the number of parallel batches so the job finishes faster.
Sort the load file by the parent Account Id so each batch touches fewer parents.
Disable field history tracking on Account.
Switch the job to serial mode if sorting is not enough.
Add a trigger that retries failed records synchronously.
questions.explain: Locks happen when parallel batches update children of the same parent. Grouping children by parent and, if needed, serial processing reduce contention.
wrong: More parallelism increases lock contention.
History tracking is unrelated to parent row locks.
Synchronous retries in a trigger add load and still hit the same locks.
questions.source: Bulk API 2.0 Developer Guide; Best Practices for Deployments with Large Data Volumes

questions.q: A company is about to restructure its role hierarchy and add many sharing rules, then reload 2M records. How can they reduce the time spent on sharing recalculation?
options: Run the changes in a Queueable to get higher limits.
Use the Defer Sharing Calculations feature, make the changes, then resume and recalculate once.
Temporarily delete all sharing rules, reload the data, and recreate the rules later from a metadata backup.
Make every user a System Administrator during the load.
questions.explain: Deferring sharing calculations suspends recalculation during big changes, so it runs once at the end instead of after every change.
wrong: Apex limits don't control platform sharing recalculation.
Deleting and recreating rules is risky and still triggers recalculation.
Granting admin access is a security risk and doesn't stop recalculation.
questions.source: Best Practices for Deployments with Large Data Volumes

questions.q: In one transaction, several trigger handlers call SettingsCache.getRates(). What does the pattern below achieve?
options: It caches the rates for all users for 24 hours, like the Platform Cache org partition.
It makes the query run asynchronously.
It runs the query once per transaction and reuses the map on later calls.
It removes the query from the 50,000 row limit.
questions.explain: A static variable lives for the transaction. Lazy loading means only the first call queries; later calls reuse the map.
wrong: Statics reset every transaction; cross-user caching needs Platform Cache.
The query runs synchronously on the first call.
The rows still count once toward the limit.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Static and Instance Methods, Variables

questions.q: Currency rates come from an external service, change once a day, and are needed by every user on many pages. Which approach best reduces repeated callouts?
options: Store the rates in a static variable in the controller.
Cache the rates in the Platform Cache org partition with a TTL; call the service only on a miss.
Store the rates in the Platform Cache session partition so each user's pages read them without a new callout.
Store the rates in the Visualforce view state.
questions.explain: The org cache is shared by all users across transactions, so one callout can serve everyone until the TTL expires.
wrong: A static variable lasts only one transaction.
Session cache is per user, so every user would trigger a callout.
View state is per page instance and bloats the page.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Platform Cache

questions.q: A developer reads a value from Platform Cache and immediately uses it. Testing passes, but production sometimes throws a NullPointerException. What is the most likely reason?
questions.code:
Decimal eur = (Decimal) Cache.Org.get('local.Rates.EUR');
Decimal converted = amount * eur;
options: Org cache is only available in asynchronous Apex.
The key format is invalid; Platform Cache keys must always start with "c." instead of "local." in every org.
Cache values are always returned as strings.
Cached items can expire or be evicted at any time, so the code must handle a null and reload.
questions.explain: Platform Cache is best-effort. Code must check for null and rebuild the value (or implement Cache.CacheBuilder for automatic loading).
wrong: Org cache works in sync and async Apex.
Keys use namespace.partition.key, and local is the correct namespace for an org without one; "c." is not a cache key prefix.
get() returns the stored Object, which can be cast.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Platform Cache Best Practices

questions.q: A before-update trigger hits "Apex CPU time limit exceeded" on bulk updates. The code calls Schema.getGlobalDescribe() inside a loop and uses nested for loops to match Contacts to Accounts. Which two changes most reduce CPU time? Choose 2.
options: Replace the nested loops with a Map<Id, List<Contact>> built in one pass.
Add System.debug statements to find the slow line in production.
Get describe information once (for example Contact.SObjectType.getDescribe()) and store it in a static variable.
Move the matching logic into a SOQL query inside the loop, because database time is not counted.
Convert the trigger to an after-update trigger.
questions.explain: Map lookups turn O(n*m) work into O(n). Describing once and caching the result avoids repeating expensive describe work.
wrong: Extra debug statements add CPU time.
Queries in a loop break the SOQL limit.
After triggers do the same amount of work and would need extra DML.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits; Apex Developer Guide: Understanding Apex Describe Information

questions.q: A Lightning web component uses @wire to call an Apex method that returns a list of Accounts. What must the Apex method have?
options: @RemoteAction
@AuraEnabled only
@AuraEnabled(cacheable=true)
@InvocableMethod
questions.explain: Wired Apex methods must be marked @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true), which also enables client-side caching.
wrong: @RemoteAction is for Visualforce JavaScript remoting.
Without cacheable=true, the method can only be called imperatively.
@InvocableMethod is for Flow and Process automation.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Call Apex Methods

questions.q: A lightning-datatable must let users scroll through up to 50,000 Case records. Loading all of them at once freezes the page. What is the best approach?
options: Return all 50,000 rows from a cacheable method so the client caches them.
Use infinite loading: onloadmore fetches the next 50 rows with keyset paging (WHERE Id > :lastId ORDER BY Id).
Use SOQL OFFSET in the onloadmore handler to fetch the next 50 rows each time, all the way down to the 50,000th row.
Render 50,000 rows with a for:each template instead of the datatable.
questions.explain: Infinite loading fetches small pages as the user scrolls. Keyset pagination works at any depth, unlike OFFSET.
wrong: Sending 50,000 rows still overloads the browser and payload.
SOQL OFFSET is capped at 2,000 rows.
Rendering 50,000 DOM rows is even slower.
questions.source: Lightning Component Library: lightning-datatable; SOQL and SOSL Reference: OFFSET

questions.q: A search box in an LWC calls an Apex search method on every keystroke, causing many server round trips. What should the developer do?
options: Mark the Apex method cacheable=false.
Move the search into renderedCallback().
Switch the Apex method to @future so the searches run in the background and stop blocking the user's typing.
Debounce: restart a setTimeout on each keystroke and call Apex only after the user pauses (about 300 ms).
questions.explain: Debouncing waits until typing pauses, so one call replaces many.
wrong: Turning off caching makes things worse.
renderedCallback runs after every render and can cause loops.
Future methods can't return data to a component.
questions.source: LWC Recipes: Debounce; Trailhead: Performance Troubleshooting in LWC

questions.q: A record page loads slowly. It contains a custom LWC with four tabs, each with a heavy child component, and each child uses its own imperative Apex call to read fields from the current record. Which two changes improve performance? Choose 2.
options: Call refreshApex() every few seconds to keep the data fresh.
Render each tab's heavy child only when that tab is active, using lwc:if.
Mark the Apex methods cacheable=true and also have them update a "Last Viewed" field.
Load all four children in connectedCallback() so they are ready early.
Read the current record's fields with Lightning Data Service (getRecord) so components share one cache instead of separate Apex calls.
questions.explain: Lazy rendering avoids building hidden components. LDS caches records and shares them across components, cutting server calls.
wrong: Polling adds server load.
Cacheable methods cannot perform DML.
Loading everything up front is the cause of the slow page.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Lightning Data Service; Conditional Rendering

questions.q: What is the maximum view state size for a Visualforce page?
options: 170 KB
135 KB
6 MB
1 MB
questions.explain: View state is limited to 170 KB. Larger pages fail with a view state error.
wrong: 135 KB is not the Visualforce limit.
6 MB is not a Visualforce limit (it was the old synchronous Apex heap size).
1 MB is not the view state limit.
questions.source: Visualforce Developer Guide: Visualforce Limits

questions.q: A Visualforce controller builds a large List<ChartPoint> for a chart. The list is rebuilt on every request anyway, but it makes the view state huge. What should the developer do?
options: Move the list into a controller extension instead of the main controller.
Move the list into a hidden apex:inputText.
Declare the list with the transient keyword.
Ask Salesforce Support to raise the view state limit.
questions.explain: Transient variables are not serialized into view state. Since the list is rebuilt anyway, nothing is lost.
wrong: Non-transient extension fields are serialized into view state too.
Hidden inputs add data to the page and view state.
The view state limit can't be increased.
questions.source: Visualforce Developer Guide: Best Practices for Improving Visualforce Performance

questions.q: A read-only Visualforce page runs Apex that must loop through about 200,000 rows to compute and show statistics. It never performs DML. Which setting allows the queries to succeed?
options: Set readOnly="true" on apex:page to raise the query row limit to 1,000,000.
Set cache="true" on apex:page.
Add the transient keyword to the query results.
Use action="{!init}" on apex:page.
questions.explain: Read-only mode raises the SOQL row limit for the request to 1,000,000 rows (and iteration to 10,000 items), as long as no DML happens.
wrong: cache="true" controls browser caching, not Apex limits.
Transient reduces view state but doesn't change row limits.
An action method runs in the same limits.
questions.source: Visualforce Developer Guide: Working with Large Sets of Data

questions.q: A Visualforce page shows 8,000 Leads in one table inside an apex:form and keeps hitting view state errors. Which two changes are the best fixes? Choose 2.
options: Ask Support to increase the view state limit for the org.
Wrap every section of the page in its own apex:form.
Use a StandardSetController with setPageSize() to show one page of Leads at a time.
Store the full Lead list in an apex:inputHidden field on the page so the controller doesn't have to re-query it.
Mark data that doesn't need to survive postbacks as transient and query only the displayed fields.
questions.explain: Pagination keeps only a page of records in state, and transient fields plus fewer queried fields shrink what gets serialized.
wrong: The 170 KB limit can't be raised.
Multiple forms add view state; best practice is a single form.
Hidden fields add even more data to the page.
questions.source: Visualforce Developer Guide: Best Practices for Improving Visualforce Performance; StandardSetController

questions.q: A global search bar must find a phone fragment typed by the user in Accounts, Contacts and Leads at once. Which tool fits best?
options: One SOQL query with a relationship subquery
Three SOQL queries with LIKE '%...%'
An aggregate SOQL query
One SOSL FIND query RETURNING Account, Contact, Lead
questions.explain: SOSL searches text across multiple objects in one query using the search index.
wrong: SOQL subqueries follow relationships and can't search unrelated objects together.
Leading wildcards can't use indexes and cost three queries.
Aggregates summarize data; they don't search text.
questions.source: SOQL and SOSL Reference: Choosing between SOQL and SOSL

questions.q: A page shows total won Amount per Account. The current Apex queries 40,000 Opportunities and sums them in a loop, which is slow and uses lots of heap. What is the best improvement?
options: Use SELECT AccountId, SUM(Amount) FROM Opportunity WHERE IsWon = true GROUP BY AccountId.
Query the Opportunities in a SOQL for loop and keep summing in Apex.
Use SOSL to find won Opportunities.
Run the same loop in a @future method and return the totals to the page.
questions.explain: An aggregate query moves the summing into the database, returning one row per Account and cutting heap and CPU use.
wrong: A SOQL for loop saves heap but still does all the work in Apex.
SOSL is for text search, not summarizing.
Future methods can't return values to the page.
questions.source: SOQL and SOSL Reference: Aggregate Functions

questions.q: A developer needs Task records with the Phone of the related Account when What is an Account, and the Amount when What is an Opportunity, in one query. What should they use?
options: Two queries: one filtered on What.Type = 'Account' and one on What.Type = 'Opportunity'.
A TYPEOF What WHEN Account THEN Phone WHEN Opportunity THEN Amount END clause.
What.Phone and What.Amount directly in the SELECT list.
A GROUP BY What.Type clause.
questions.explain: TYPEOF selects different fields based on the polymorphic relationship's object type in a single query.
wrong: This works but uses two queries when one TYPEOF query is enough.
The polymorphic What relationship only exposes fields common to all its targets (such as Name), not Phone or Amount.
Grouping doesn't retrieve type-specific fields, and TYPEOF can't be used with GROUP BY.
questions.source: SOQL and SOSL Reference: TYPEOF

questions.q: When users save an Order, an after-update trigger makes a callout to an ERP and runs a heavy recalculation over related records. Users see long saves and CPU timeouts. Which two designs move the work out of the user's transaction? Choose 2.
options: Ask Salesforce Support to raise the synchronous CPU limit.
Move the trigger logic into a before-update trigger.
Enqueue a Queueable class that implements Database.AllowsCallouts to do the callout.
Make the callout directly in the trigger and catch CalloutException.
Publish a platform event and do the recalculation in a platform event trigger, which runs in its own transaction.
questions.explain: A Queueable with Database.AllowsCallouts runs async with higher limits and can call out. A platform event subscriber runs separately, decoupling the recalculation from the save.
wrong: Governor limits can't be raised by Support.
Before triggers run in the same transaction and can't make callouts either.
Callouts aren't allowed synchronously from triggers.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Queueable Apex; Platform Events Developer Guide

questions.q: A service console LWC shows shipment status from a carrier API that often takes 20+ seconds to answer. The developer rewrote the Apex to return a Continuation, but the component now gets an error instead of the status. The org has 4,000 agents. Which two changes are required? Choose 2.
options: Change the timeout to 180 seconds so slow carrier responses are not cut off.
Make handleTracking an instance method in a separate CarrierCallbacks class.
Add continuation=true to the @AuraEnabled annotation on startTracking.
Add a Remote Site Setting for the carrier, because named credentials are not supported in continuations.
Import the method from @salesforce/apexContinuation/ShipmentController.startTracking.
questions.explain: An Apex method that returns a Continuation must be annotated with @AuraEnabled(continuation=true), and the LWC must use the @salesforce/apexContinuation import syntax so the framework knows the method can return a continuation.
wrong: The maximum timeout for a single continuation is 120 seconds.
The callback method must be in the same Apex class that creates the Continuation.
A named credential endpoint works with continuations and removes the need for a Remote Site Setting.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Apex Continuation Object; @AuraEnabled Annotations for Continuations; Continuations Example

questions.q: An LWC calls a warranty service through a continuation. To audit usage, a developer adds a log insert to the method that builds the continuation. Users now always see an error and no warranty data. What explains this, and what is the fix?
options: The insert leaves uncommitted work before the callout; wrap it in a Savepoint and roll back before returning con.
DML in a method that returns a Continuation stops it and rolls back; move the insert into processWarranty.
Continuation methods run in a read-only context; publish a platform event instead of inserting.
The insert counts against the three-callout limit of the continuation; reduce the requests to two.
questions.explain: An Apex method that returns a Continuation can't perform DML. If it does, the continuation doesn't proceed, the transaction is rolled back and an error is returned. DML is allowed in the callback method.
wrong: A savepoint and rollback would discard the log and still uses DML statements in the continuation method.
The rule is specifically "no DML in the method that returns the Continuation", and the callback can do DML; a platform event workaround is not the documented fix.
DML does not count toward the callout limit; the three-request limit is about HttpRequest objects.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Continuation Limits

questions.q: A Visualforce page used by field technicians calls a parts-availability service with a Continuation. The controller also loads the technician's last 3,000 work orders into a public list for a summary panel. The continuation now fails with a controller-state size error, although the page view state is well under its limit. What is the best fix?
options: Raise the continuation timeout to 120 seconds so the controller can be serialized in time.
Move the callout into a @future(callout=true) method so the controller is never serialized and the page isn't blocked.
Split the callout into three parallel requests so each serialized state is smaller.
Mark history transient and rebuild it when needed; the controller is serialized for the continuation (80 KB limit).
questions.explain: When a continuation executes, all involved controllers are serialized, and that controller state is limited to 80 KB, separate from the 170 KB view state limit. Transient members are not serialized, so marking the large list transient shrinks the controller state.
wrong: The timeout controls how long the callout may run, not the size of the serialized controller.
Future methods can't return a result to the waiting Visualforce request, so the page would lose the asynchronous response it needs.
All requests share the same serialized controller; adding requests does not reduce its size.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Asynchronous Callout Limits

questions.q: An architect is reviewing a proposal to convert several LWC Apex callouts to continuations. Which two statements about continuations are accurate? Choose 2.
options: Continuation callouts are not boxcar'ed with other actions, so they don't block other server actions from the component while they run.
Since Winter '20, all callouts are excluded from the long-running request limit, so the main reason to use continuations now is a better user experience.
The callback runs in an asynchronous transaction, so it gets 200 SOQL queries and 60 seconds of CPU.
A component can start several continuations at the same moment, and the client runs them in parallel.
A continuation raises the per-callout timeout to 10 minutes, matching the maximum Apex transaction time.
questions.explain: The framework treats continuations as background actions that are not boxcar'ed, so they don't block other actions. Since Winter '20 regular callouts no longer count toward the long-running request limit either, so continuations are recommended mainly for user experience.
wrong: When the continuation returns, a new Apex transaction starts with the normal limits reset; it does not get asynchronous limits.
Actions containing a continuation are processed serially from the client; only one continuation can be in progress at a time.
The maximum timeout for a single continuation is 120 seconds.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Make Long-Running Callouts with Continuations; Continuation Limits; Apex Developer Guide: Asynchronous Callout Limits

questions.q: A developer writes a test for a Visualforce controller that uses a Continuation (the controller stores the label returned by addHttpRequest in requestLabel). The test sets an HttpCalloutMock, calls startRequest(), and asserts that controller.result is set, but result is always null. Which change makes the test exercise the callback with a mock response?
options: Wrap startRequest() in Test.startTest() and Test.stopTest() so the queued asynchronous callout and callback finish before the assert.
Call ctrl.processResponse() directly after startRequest(), because the mock already stored the response.
Set a mock with Test.setContinuationResponse(ctrl.requestLabel, res), then call Test.invokeContinuationMethod(ctrl, con).
Replace HttpCalloutMock with WebServiceMock, because continuations are processed as SOAP calls.
questions.explain: Continuation callouts are simulated with Test.setContinuationResponse() to set the mock response for a request label and Test.invokeContinuationMethod() to run the callback. The callback then processes the mock response.
wrong: stopTest() runs queued async Apex, but it does not execute a continuation callback.
Without Test.setContinuationResponse there is no response for Continuation.getResponse() to return.
HttpRequest-based continuations are not SOAP calls, and setMock does not drive the continuation callback either way.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Testing Asynchronous Callouts

questions.q: A product page LWC uses @wire to call a continuation that fetches live pricing. The org has 600,000 products and the pricing service is slow. The Apex below compiles, but at runtime the wire returns an error. What is the cause?
options: The space between continuation=true and cacheable=true must be a comma.
The callback must not be static when it is used from an LWC; make processPricing an instance method instead.
con.state can hold only a Map<String, Object>, not a String.
The callback lacks cacheable=true; if the continuation method is cacheable, the callback must be too.
questions.explain: If the method returning the Continuation is cacheable=true but the callback is not, the combination is invalid and throws an exception. Every method in the continuation chain must be cacheable=true to use @wire.
wrong: The documented syntax uses a space, not a comma, between continuation=true and cacheable=true.
The LWC continuation examples use a static callback with (List<String> labels, Object state) parameters.
The state property is of type Object, so any supported Apex type, including a String, can be passed.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: @AuraEnabled Annotations for Continuations

questions.q: A team builds a shared trigger framework so every object handler reuses the same dispatch logic. A developer writes LeadHandler, but the class fails to save. Which change fixes it while keeping the framework reusable?
options: Add the override keyword: protected override void beforeInsert(List<SObject> recs).
Declare LeadHandler as virtual so it may redefine methods from its parent.
Change TriggerHandler to an interface so LeadHandler can implement beforeInsert.
Mark beforeInsert as static in both classes so the trigger can call it without an instance.
questions.explain: A subclass that redefines a virtual method must use the override keyword. With override, run() in the base class calls LeadHandler's version polymorphically, so the dispatch logic stays shared.
wrong: Making the child virtual only allows further extension; the redefined method still needs override.
An interface can't hold the shared run() implementation, so the dispatch logic would be duplicated in every handler.
Static methods are not overridden polymorphically, so run() would never call the Lead logic.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Extending a Class; Apex Class Definition

questions.q: A retailer calculates discounts differently for Web, Store and Partner orders, and marketing adds a new channel every quarter. Today the logic is a 400-line if/else block copied into three classes. The team wants to add a channel without editing or redeploying the calling code. Which two design choices support this? Choose 2.
options: Move the if/else block into one static utility method and call it from all three classes, so the logic lives in one place.
Define a DiscountCalculator interface with a calculate(Order__c o) method and one implementing class per channel.
Copy the logic into a trigger on each channel's record type so each team owns its copy.
Store the implementing class name per channel in custom metadata and create it with Type.forName(name).newInstance().
Declare every channel class global so any code in the org can call it directly.
questions.explain: An interface lets callers depend on one contract while each channel has its own implementation. Resolving the class name from custom metadata with Type.forName() means a new channel is a new class plus a metadata record, with no change to the caller.
wrong: Centralizing helps reuse, but every new channel still means editing the same if/else method.
Copying logic per trigger increases duplication and makes every change harder.
Global access only widens visibility; callers would still need code changes for each new class.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Interfaces; Apex Reference Guide: Type Class

questions.q: To keep a pricing feature in one file, a developer nests helper classes inside a PricingService class. The class won't compile. Which line causes the error?
options: Line 2, because an inner class must declare with sharing or without sharing.
Line 8, because an inner class can't be private.
Line 4, because Apex allows inner classes only one level deep.
Line 3, because inner classes can't declare instance fields.
questions.explain: Apex supports inner classes only one level deep, so LineItem inside Quote fails. Move LineItem up to be a sibling inner class or into its own top-level class.
wrong: Sharing keywords are optional on inner classes.
Private is the default access for inner classes and is allowed.
Inner classes can have instance fields; Quote.total is valid.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Apex Class Definition

questions.q: The same Account query, with slightly different field lists, appears in 14 classes. When a new field was added to a page, three classes threw "SObject row was retrieved via SOQL without querying the requested field". The team wants one place to own Account queries and keep business rules out of controllers. What is the best design?
options: Create an AccountsSelector class (e.g. selectByIds(Set<Id>)) that owns the field list, called from a service layer.
Query Account with FIELDS(ALL) everywhere so no field is ever missing.
Store the query string in a custom label and run it with Database.query() in each class, so editing the label fixes all 14.
Add every Account field to each query and cache the results in a static variable in every class.
questions.explain: A selector class centralizes queries and field lists, so every caller gets the same fields and changes happen once. A service layer on top keeps business logic reusable across UI, triggers and batch code.
wrong: FIELDS(ALL) is limited to 200 rows and returns far more data than needed, hurting heap and performance.
Each class still runs and maintains its own query call, and dynamic SOQL from a label is harder to test and secure.
Querying every field wastes heap and rows, and per-class caches still duplicate the logic.
questions.source: Trailhead: Apex Enterprise Patterns: Service Layer; Apex Enterprise Patterns: Data Mapper (Selector) Layer

questions.q: A team creates a service component c/dateUtils (JavaScript only, no template) to share date formatting across 20 LWCs. The first component that uses it fails: formatDue is not available where taskList calls it. Which change fixes it?
options: Add a dateUtils.html file, because every LWC module needs a template.
Change the import to a named import: import { formatDue } from 'c/dateUtils';
Decorate formatDue with @api so other components can call it.
Set isExposed to true in dateUtils.js-meta.xml so other components can import it.
questions.explain: dateUtils exports formatDue as a named export, so it must be imported with braces. A default import looks for a default export that doesn't exist.
wrong: A service component that only shares JavaScript doesn't need a template.
@api is for public properties and methods of a component class, not for exported module functions.
isExposed controls App Builder and similar targets, not whether other LWCs can import the module.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Share JavaScript Code

questions.q: In a legacy Aura app, a developer moves a shared header and spinner into a base component so 12 page components can reuse it. The sub component compiles, but its own markup never appears on the page; only the header shows. What is the fix?
questions.code: {!v.title}
options: Add abstract="true" to c:basePage so sub components can add markup.
Move <c:orderTable/> inside <aura:set attribute="title">.
Add {!v.body} to the markup of c:basePage where the sub component's content should render.
Add implements="c:basePage" to c:orderPage instead of extends.
questions.explain: Free markup in a sub component becomes its body and is passed to the super component. The super component outputs it only where it includes {!v.body}.
wrong: abstract only stops the base from being used directly; the body still needs {!v.body} to render.
The title attribute is a String; putting a component inside it would not render it as body.
implements is for interfaces; a component is reused through extends.
questions.source: Lightning Aura Components Developer Guide: Inherited Component Attributes

questions.q: A company is planning which reuse techniques to use while it still maintains Aura components and builds new LWCs. Which two statements are correct? Choose 2.
options: An Aura interface can include a client-side controller with shared logic for implementing components.
An Aura interface can extend only one other interface.
A sub component can't set inherited attribute values; it must redefine each attribute.
An Aura component can extend only one extensible component but can implement multiple interfaces.
LWCs can share logic by importing functions exported from a JavaScript-only service component.
questions.explain: Aura allows one extends and multiple implements for components. In LWC, shared code lives in ES modules (service components) that other components import.
wrong: Interfaces can contain only attributes, registered events and methods; no controllers, renderers or markup.
An Aura interface can extend multiple interfaces using a comma-separated list.
A sub component uses <aura:set> to set inherited attribute values from its super component.
questions.source: Lightning Aura Components Developer Guide: Interfaces; Inheritance Rules; Inherited Component Attributes

questions.q: An integration inserts 150 Contacts in one API call. 80 of them belong to Accounts in the Banking industry, and every mailing state has a Territory__c record. No other automation runs on Contact. How many SOQL queries does this trigger use, and does the load succeed?
options: 2 queries; it succeeds because the Territory query runs once per transaction.
151 queries; it fails with "Too many SOQL queries: 101".
81 queries; it succeeds, but a load with more than 99 Banking Contacts would fail.
1 query; inline queries in a loop over Trigger.new are batched by the platform.
questions.explain: One query builds the Account map, then one Territory query runs for each of the 80 Banking Contacts: 81 in total, under the 100 limit. With 100 or more Banking Contacts it would pass 100 and fail, so the Territory lookup should also be moved into a Map built before the loop.
wrong: The Territory query is inside the loop and runs once per matching Contact.
Only Banking Contacts run the inner query, so it is 81, not 151.
The platform does not batch SOQL statements written inside loops.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits; Bulk Apex Triggers

questions.q: A one-time Anonymous Apex script inserts 450 Leads in a single insert statement. The after-insert trigger below creates a follow-up Task per Lead. No other automation exists on Lead or Task. How many SOQL queries and DML statements does the whole transaction use?
options: 1 SOQL query and 2 DML statements
3 SOQL queries and 3 DML statements
450 SOQL queries and 451 DML statements
3 SOQL queries and 4 DML statements
questions.explain: The trigger runs in chunks of 200 records, so it fires three times (200, 200, 50) in the same transaction. Each run issues one query and one insert: 3 queries, plus the script's insert and three Task inserts for 4 DML statements.
wrong: The trigger runs once per 200-record chunk, not once per DML statement.
This forgets the Anonymous Apex insert of the Leads, which is also a DML statement.
The code is bulkified; it does not query or insert per record.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Bulk Triggers; Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A synchronous Apex method prepares a territory review. It returns 400 Accounts for a region, and each Account has about 150 Contacts. The method fails even though it runs only one query. What is the cause?
options: Subquery child rows count toward the 50,000 query-row limit: 400 + about 60,000 rows is too many.
A parent-child subquery counts as 300 queries, one per parent row, exceeding the 100-query limit.
Subqueries are limited to 2,000 child rows per query in Apex, so the query fails at the 2,001st Contact.
Subqueries can't be used in synchronous Apex on more than 200 parent records.
questions.explain: Row counts from relationship subqueries contribute to the total query rows for the transaction. About 60,400 rows passes the 50,000 limit, so the code should filter Contacts, split the work, or use Batch Apex.
wrong: Each parent-child relationship counts as one extra query toward a separate, higher limit, not one query per parent row.
There is no 2,000-child-row cap on a subquery in Apex; 2,000 is the SOSL row limit and the OFFSET maximum.
There is no 200-parent rule for subqueries.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A developer adds instrumentation to an Apex method that onboards a new customer. All operations succeed and no triggers exist on these objects. The contacts list has 120 records. What does the debug statement print?
questions.explain: Database.setSavepoint() counts as a DML statement, and so do the two inserts and the update: 4. Inserting a list of 120 Contacts is one statement (it adds 120 DML rows, not 120 statements).
wrong: This misses that Database.setSavepoint() counts against the DML statement limit.
A list insert is one DML statement no matter how many records it holds.
A list insert counts once; rows are tracked by a separate 10,000-row limit.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A before-insert trigger on Lead flags duplicates against existing Contacts by email. Loads of 200 Leads compared with 9,000 matching Contacts hit "Apex CPU time limit exceeded". Which refactor of the matching loop is the most efficient?
options: Move the nested loops into a @future method so they run with the 60,000 ms asynchronous CPU limit instead of 10,000.
Add a break after a match so the inner loop stops early.
Run a separate query per Lead with WHERE Email = :l.Email LIMIT 1 instead of looping.
Build a Map<String, Id> of email to Contact Id once, then set each Lead's field with byEmail.get(l.Email).
questions.explain: The nested loops do up to 200 × 9,000 comparisons. A map keyed by email turns each lookup into one operation, so CPU grows with records, not records squared.
wrong: A before trigger must set fields in the same transaction; a future method can't change Trigger.new, and it hides the inefficiency.
break helps only after a match and still scans the list for every Lead in the worst case.
One query per Lead hits the 100-query limit in a 200-record load.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Bulk Apex Triggers; Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: An after-update trigger on Opportunity sets Last_Win__c on the parent Account when an Opportunity is Closed Won. A nightly job closes 200 Opportunities that belong to about 40 Accounts, and it fails. Which two changes produce a correct, bulkified trigger? Choose 2.
options: Add each Account to a List<Account> inside the loop and run a single update on that list after the loop finishes.
Drop the query and build new Account(Id = o.AccountId, Last_Win__c = o.CloseDate), since the Id is on each Opportunity.
Wrap the update in Database.update(a, false) so failed records are skipped.
Move the loop body into a @future method called once per Opportunity.
Put the Accounts in a Map<Id, Account> keyed by Account Id and run one update on map.values() after the loop.
questions.explain: The Account Id is already on each Opportunity, so no query is needed: an Account built with just its Id can be updated. Keying by Id in a Map removes duplicates, so one update on map.values() never hits "Duplicate id in list".
wrong: Several Opportunities share an Account, so a List would contain the same Id more than once and the update fails with a duplicate id error.
Partial success does not fix the query and DML inside the loop.
Up to 200 future calls exceeds the 50-per-transaction future limit and adds overhead.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Bulk Apex Triggers; Maps of sObjects

questions.q: A Policy__c object has 3,000,000 records. Support created a custom index on Agency_Code__c. A trigger runs a query filtered only on Agency_Code__c, and for the busiest agency the filter matches 180,000 records. How does the optimizer treat this filter?
questions.code:
SELECT Id, Premium__c
FROM Policy__c
WHERE Agency_Code__c = :agencyCode
options: Not selective, because it matches more than 10% of the first million records (100,000).
Selective: the custom-index threshold is 10% of the first million plus 5% of the other 2 million (200,000).
Not selective, because custom-indexed filters must match fewer than 30,000 records on objects over 1 million rows.
Selective only if a standard index exists, because custom indexes are used only for reports.
questions.explain: For custom indexes the threshold is 10% of the first million records and 5% of records after that: 100,000 + 100,000 = 200,000. 180,000 is under it, so the index can be used.
wrong: The 10% applies only to the first million; records beyond that add 5% each to the threshold.
There is no 30,000-row threshold for custom indexes.
Custom indexes are considered for SOQL, reports and list views.
questions.source: Best Practices for Deployments with Large Data Volumes: Indexes

questions.q: A query on Claim__c (4 million rows) is slow and fails in a trigger. Status__c has a custom index; Adjuster_Region__c is a plain Text field. Each filter alone matches about 2% of rows. Which two changes let the optimizer use indexes? Choose 2.
questions.code:
SELECT Id, Amount__c
FROM Claim__c
WHERE Status__c = 'Escalated'
   OR Adjuster_Region__c = 'North'
options: Swap the order of the two OR conditions so the indexed field is evaluated first.
Ask Salesforce Support for a custom index on Adjuster_Region__c, because every field in an OR must be indexed.
Add AND Adjuster_Region__c != null to narrow the results.
Split it into two queries, one per condition, and combine the results in Apex.
Add LIMIT 50000 so the query never returns too many rows.
questions.explain: For OR, all fields in the OR must be indexed for any index to be used. Indexing the second field, or decomposing the query into two selective queries and merging the results, lets each part use an index.
wrong: The optimizer does not depend on the order of OR conditions.
Negative filters like != null can't use an index and don't make the OR selective.
LIMIT caps the result size but does not make a non-selective filter use an index.
questions.source: Best Practices for Deployments with Large Data Volumes: Indexes; SOQL and SOSL best practices

questions.q: A developer checks a query on Invoice__c in the Developer Console Query Plan tool before using it in a trigger. Invoice__c has 2,400,000 rows. The tool returns the plans below. What should the developer conclude?
questions.code:
Cardinality  Fields      Leading Operation  Cost   sObject Cardinality
310000       -           TableScan          1.38   2400000
310000       Status__c   Index              2.10   2400000
options: The query uses the Status__c index, because an Index plan is always chosen over a TableScan.
The query is selective, because both plans return the same cardinality.
The query is selective, because the plan cost of 1.38 is under the 2,400,000-row sObject cardinality.
No plan costs less than 1, so the query is not selective and can fail in a trigger on this object.
questions.explain: The optimizer picks the lowest-cost plan, here the TableScan. A cost above 1 means the query is not selective, so it needs a more selective indexed filter before it runs in a trigger on a table this size.
wrong: The optimizer chooses the lowest-cost plan, and the Index plan costs more here.
Equal cardinality does not make a query selective; cost is what matters.
Cost is compared with 1, not with the number of rows.
questions.source: Developer Console Query Plan Tool FAQ

questions.q: Code__c on Product_Batch__c (1.5M rows) is a Text field marked as External ID. Index tables don't include null values by default. Which two WHERE clauses can the optimizer drive from the Code__c index, assuming each matches only a few hundred rows? Choose 2.
options: A
B
C
D
E
questions.explain: Equality and IN filters on an External ID field can use its index when they match few rows. Negative operators, leading wildcards and null comparisons can't use a default custom index.
wrong: Negative operators such as != can't use an index.
A leading wildcard can't use the index; it needs a scan.
Custom index tables don't include nulls unless Support enables that, so = null can't use the default index.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Working with Very Large SOQL Queries; Best Practices for Deployments with Large Data Volumes: Indexes

questions.q: A trigger on Subscription__c (2M rows) finds renewals due this month by filtering on a formula field. The formula is Days_To_Renewal__c = Renewal_Date__c - TODAY(). Support says they can't index the field. What is the best way to make the query selective?
questions.code:
SELECT Id FROM Subscription__c
WHERE Days_To_Renewal__c >= 0
  AND Days_To_Renewal__c <= 30
options: Add ORDER BY Days_To_Renewal__c so the optimizer can sort the rows by the formula value before it filters them.
Filter on Renewal_Date__c directly (>= :today AND <= :today.addDays(30)) and have it indexed if needed.
Mark the formula field as an External ID so it is indexed automatically.
Wrap the query in a SOQL for loop so it processes fewer rows at a time.
questions.explain: Formulas that use TODAY() are non-deterministic and can't be indexed. Filtering on the underlying date field, which can be indexed, keeps the query selective.
wrong: Sorting doesn't make a filter selective and can add cost.
Formula fields can't be marked as External ID.
A SOQL for loop reduces heap, not the rows the database must scan to evaluate the filter.
questions.source: Best Practices for Deployments with Large Data Volumes: Indexes; SOQL and SOSL best practices

questions.q: A logistics company has 40 million Shipment__c records. Its weekly dashboard reports read the same 15 fields, mixing standard and custom fields, and run slowly. A consultant suggests skinny tables. Which two statements about skinny tables are true? Choose 2.
options: An admin creates and edits them in Setup under Object Manager.
They hold standard and custom fields together, so reads that use only those fields avoid a database join.
They are copied automatically to every sandbox type.
They include soft-deleted records so Recycle Bin reports run faster.
They can't contain fields from other objects, such as the parent Account's Region.
questions.explain: A skinny table combines standard and custom fields of one object, so read-only operations on those fields skip the join between the two underlying tables. It can't include fields from other objects.
wrong: Skinny tables are created by Salesforce Customer Support; you can't create or modify them yourself.
They are copied to Full sandboxes only; other sandbox types need a Support request.
Skinny tables omit soft-deleted records.
questions.source: Best Practices for Deployments with Large Data Volumes: Skinny Tables

questions.q: A data warehouse team must extract all 80 million Activity_Log__c records every quarter with Bulk API (version 1.0). Single extract batches time out. What should they do?
options: Run the extract with the REST API query endpoint and queryMore so each call returns 2,000 rows.
Add OFFSET clauses in steps of 2,000 to split the query.
Enable PK chunking (Sforce-Enable-PKChunking header) to split the query into Id-range batches.
Create a skinny table so the extract reads fewer columns.
questions.explain: PK chunking splits a bulk query on a large table into chunks by record Id range, each processed as a separate batch. The default chunk size is 100,000 and the maximum is 250,000.
wrong: Paging 80 million rows 2,000 at a time through the REST API is far slower and uses many API calls.
OFFSET is capped at 2,000 rows, so it can't page through 80 million records.
Skinny tables speed reports and queries on selected fields, but they don't split a massive extract into batches.
questions.source: Bulk API Developer Guide: PK Chunking

questions.q: An after-update trigger on Case updates sibling Cases that share a Parent. In bulk loads the same records are processed again and again, and the transaction fails with "Apex CPU time limit exceeded". Which change best fixes the repeated work?
options: Keep a static Set<Id> of processed Case Ids in CaseService, skip Ids already in it, and add new Ids before the update.
Use a static Boolean that is set to true on the first run and blocks every later run in the transaction.
Move the update into a Queueable that re-enqueues itself until no siblings remain.
Change the trigger to before update so the update statement is no longer needed.
questions.explain: A static set of processed Ids persists for the transaction, so each record is handled once and the recursion stops. Unlike a single Boolean, it still processes records from later 200-record chunks.
wrong: A single Boolean also skips legitimate records in later trigger chunks of the same bulk operation.
Self-chaining Queueables move the loop to async and can run endlessly; they don't remove the repeated work.
A before trigger can change only the records being saved, not their siblings.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Static and Instance Methods, Variables, and Initialization Code; Triggers and Order of Execution

questions.q: A nightly job started from a Schedulable totals Usage__c per Category__c on Asset__c and writes the totals to 12 Usage_Summary__c records. It was changed from a plain List query to a SOQL for loop to fix heap errors, which worked. The object has now grown to 62,000 active rows and the job fails again. What is happening and what is the best fix?
options: Replace the loop with SELECT Category__c, SUM(Usage__c) ... GROUP BY Category__c, so only 12 rows count toward the limit.
SOQL for loops still count every row toward the 50,000 limit; use Batch Apex with Database.Stateful running totals.
The for loop retrieves chunks of 2,000 rows, so the heap limit is hit again; switch to the single-record loop form.
Scheduled Apex gets asynchronous limits, so raise the row limit with Database.DMLOptions.
questions.explain: A SOQL for loop saves heap, but every retrieved row still counts toward the 50,000-row limit. Batch Apex with Database.getQueryLocator can process up to 50 million records, with each batch in its own transaction.
wrong: Aggregate functions other than COUNT() count every row used in the aggregation as a query row, so SUM over 62,000 rows still exceeds 50,000.
The list form of a SOQL for loop returns 200 records per chunk, and the failure here is the row limit, not heap.
Scheduled Apex runs with synchronous limits, and DMLOptions has nothing to do with query rows.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: SOQL For Loops; Working with Aggregate SOQL Queries; Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: To avoid re-querying sales territories on every page load, a developer implements Cache.CacheBuilder and reads the value with Cache.Org.get(TerritoryCache.class, regionCode). The class fails to save. What is wrong?
options: doLoad must not be static; Salesforce creates an instance of the class and calls doLoad on it.
doLoad must return a Map<String, Object>, not a List of records.
The class must call Cache.Org.put() inside doLoad to store the result.
doLoad must take no parameters, because the cache key comes from the class name only.
questions.explain: The class that implements CacheBuilder must be non-static: Salesforce instantiates it and runs doLoad(String var) to build the value. A static method does not implement the interface method.
wrong: doLoad can return any value, including a List of records.
With CacheBuilder you don't call put(); Salesforce caches what doLoad returns.
doLoad must take a String parameter, which Salesforce combines with the class name to build the key.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Safely Cache Values with the CacheBuilder Interface

questions.q: An admin created an org cache partition named Rates in an org with no namespace and made it the only partition. A developer wants to cache a Decimal exchange rate from Apex for all users. Which two snippets correctly store the value in that partition? Choose 2.
options: Cache.Session.put('local.Rates.usdEur', 1.08); // shared with all users
Cache.Org.put('local.Rates.usdEur', 1.08, 259200); // keep 3 days
Cache.Org.put('local.Rates.usdEur', 1.08);
Decimal r = Cache.Org.get('local.Rates.usdEur'); // read it back

Cache.OrgPartition p = Cache.Org.getPartition('local.Rates');
p.put('usdEur', 1.08);
questions.explain: Org cache keys use the namespace.partition.key format, with local meaning the current org's namespace. Alternatively, get the partition with Cache.Org.getPartition('local.Rates') and put using just the key.
wrong: Session cache is per user session, not shared with all users.
The maximum org cache time-to-live is 172,800 seconds (48 hours), so 3 days is not a valid TTL.
This reads rather than stores, and get() returns Object, so it must be cast: (Decimal) Cache.Org.get(...).
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Store and Retrieve Values from the Org Cache; Platform Cache Limits

questions.q: A developer caches the full product catalog (about 9,000 records with descriptions) for a quoting tool. Testing with 200 products works, but in production the put fails. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The org cache stores only primitive values such as String, Integer and Decimal; serialize the list with JSON.serialize() first.
The key must be under 20 characters; shorten it.
Org cache puts are not allowed from synchronous Apex; use a Queueable.
Each cached item is limited to 100 KB; split the catalog into smaller items (e.g. by Family) with only needed fields.
questions.explain: Each cached item is limited to 100 KB. Splitting a large list into a few reasonably large items, each under the limit, follows the Platform Cache best practices.
wrong: Org cache can store any serializable Apex object, including lists of sObjects.
The maximum key size is 50 characters, and this key is shorter than that.
Synchronous Apex can put to the org cache.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Platform Cache Best Practices; Platform Cache Limits

questions.q: An LWC shows 5,000 open Cases with a filter box and a sorted, grouped view. Typing in the box is laggy. Profiling shows sortedGroups runs several times per keystroke because the template references it in three places. What is the best fix?
options: Mark sortedGroups with @api so the engine caches its value between renders.
Compute the groups once when the data or filter changes (debounced), store them in a field, and bind the template to it.
Move the filtering into renderedCallback() so it runs after the DOM is ready.
Wrap the getter in @wire so the computed list is stored in the Lightning Data Service cache and reused on every later render.
questions.explain: Getters run every time the template reads them on each render, so heavy work in a getter repeats. Computing once when inputs change, and debouncing the input, keeps renders cheap.
wrong: @api makes a property public; it doesn't memoize a getter.
Changing tracked state in renderedCallback() triggers another render and can cause loops.
@wire works with wire adapters such as Apex methods, not with local getters.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Getters and Setters; Reactivity; Lightning Web Components Performance best practices

questions.q: An account page LWC has a "Show forecast" toggle. The forecast child calls three wired Apex methods. Users who never open the forecast still wait for those calls, and the page is slow. Why, and what fixes it?
questions.code: // JS get forecastClass() { return this.showForecast ? '' : 'slds-hide'; }
options: slds-hide only hides it with CSS, so the child and its wires still run; wrap it in <template lwc:if={showForecast}>.
The child's wires run because record-id is passed; pass recordId only after the toggle is on, and keep the CSS class.
Add the lazy attribute to <c-forecast-panel> so the engine defers its constructor and connectedCallback until visible.
Switch the three wired methods to cacheable=false so they wait until the panel is visible.
questions.explain: CSS hiding keeps the component in the DOM, so it is constructed and its wire adapters provision data. lwc:if removes and inserts the elements, so the child and its calls exist only when the toggle is on.
wrong: A wire with an undefined config property doesn't provision, but the component is still created; lwc:if is the clean fix.
LWC has no lazy attribute for child components.
Wired Apex methods must be cacheable=true, and visibility has no effect on when they run.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Render DOM Elements Conditionally; Understand the Wire Service

questions.q: A lightning-datatable loads Invoices 50 rows at a time with infinite loading and keyset paging. After the last page, the spinner keeps flashing and the server is called again and again with the same lastId. Which change fixes it?
questions.code:
<lightning-datatable key-field="Id" data={rows} columns={cols}
    enable-infinite-loading={canLoadMore}
    onloadmore={loadMore}></lightning-datatable>

// JS
canLoadMore = true;
async loadMore(event) {
    event.target.isLoading = true;
    const page = await getInvoices({ lastId: this.lastId, pageSize: 50 });
    this.rows = [...this.rows, ...page];
    if (page.length) this.lastId = page[page.length - 1].Id;
    event.target.isLoading = false;
}
options: Use OFFSET in getInvoices instead of lastId so each call returns a different page.
Raise pageSize to 2,000 so all invoices arrive in fewer calls.
Set canLoadMore = false when the returned page has fewer than 50 rows, so the table stops firing loadmore.
Remove event.target.isLoading so the table doesn't re-fire the event.
questions.explain: The table keeps firing loadmore while infinite loading is enabled and the user is near the bottom. Turning enable-infinite-loading off when a short page shows there is no more data stops the repeated calls.
wrong: OFFSET is capped at 2,000 and doesn't solve the end-of-data condition.
Bigger pages delay the problem and make each call heavier; the loop still repeats at the end.
isLoading shows the spinner and prevents overlapping loads; removing it makes duplicate calls more likely.
questions.source: Lightning Component Library: lightning-datatable (Loading More Data)

questions.q: An LWC lists a user's open Opportunities with @wire to a cacheable Apex method. After the user closes one through an imperative Apex call, the list still shows it as open until a full page reload. Which change refreshes the list correctly?
options: Call refreshApex(this.opps) after closeOpp, because opps holds the wired data.
Set cacheable=false on getOpenOpps so the wire never caches results.
Call getOpenOpps imperatively after closeOpp and assign the result, because imperative calls always bypass the client cache.
Keep the whole provisioned value (this.wiredResult = result) and call refreshApex(this.wiredResult) after closeOpp.
questions.explain: refreshApex() needs the exact object emitted by the Apex @wire. Keeping the provisioned value and refreshing it after the update re-fetches the data and updates the cache.
wrong: refreshApex needs the object emitted by the wire, not the data array copied from it.
A method must be cacheable=true to be used with @wire.
Imperative calls to a cacheable method can return cached data, and this leaves the wired list stale.
questions.source: LWC Developer Guide: Client-Side Caching of Apex Method Results; Refresh the Cache

questions.q: To cut view state, a developer marks the results list on a Visualforce search page as transient. The first search shows results, but clicking Next Page shows an empty table. What explains this?
options: Transient fields are cleared only for read-only pages; the page needs readOnly="true".
Transient fields aren't saved in view state, so results is null after the postback; nextPage must re-run the query.
Transient fields can't have getters and setters, so the apex:pageBlockTable on the page can't bind to results at all.
pageNo is also transient by default because it is an Integer, so the page resets to 0.
questions.explain: Transient variables are not part of the view state, so they are not restored on the next request. Any data needed after a postback must be recalculated, here by re-querying the page in nextPage.
wrong: transient works on any page; read-only mode is unrelated.
Transient properties can have accessors; they just aren't serialized.
Only fields marked transient are excluded; pageNo is kept in view state.
questions.source: Visualforce Developer Guide: Best Practices for Improving Visualforce Performance; Apex Developer Guide: Using the transient Keyword
